stimulus.text:
Dunmore: “And I do hereby further declare all indentured Servants, Negroes, or others, (appertaining to Rebels,) free that are able and willing to bear Arms, they joining His MAJESTY'S Troops as soon as may be, for the more speedily reducing this Colony to a proper Sense of their Duty, to His MAJESTY'S Crown and Dignity.” — Lord Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775 (abridged)

Virginia Convention: “We think it proper to declare, that all slaves who have been, or shall be seduced, by his lordship's proclamation, or other arts, to desert their masters' service, and take up arms against the inhabitants of this colony, shall be liable to such punishment as shall hereafter be directed by the General Convention. . . . we hereby promise pardon to them, they surrendering themselves to Col. William Woodford, or any other commander of our troops, and not appearing in arms after the publication hereof.” — Virginia Convention, December 14, 1775 (abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Lord Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775, and Virginia Convention declaration, December 14, 1775. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Lord Dunmore's Proclamation (November 7, 1775) and the Virginia Convention's reply (December 14, 1775), public domain. Different questions from the 3.5 Dunmore set (0510-0512).

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, A. The Call for Egalitarianism

stem: Both Dunmore and the Virginia Convention made offers to enslaved people most directly because

options.text: Both sides had agreed that slavery was wrong and should end at once
options.misconception: Neither side proposes ending slavery; Dunmore offers freedom only for service, and Virginia offers only pardon for return to bondage.

options.text: Enslaved people's choices could decide the war, so each side bid for them
Parliament had ordered both sides to free their enslaved workers
options.misconception: Parliament ordered no such thing; Dunmore acted on his own authority as governor, and Virginia acted to protect slavery.

options.text: The Continental Congress had promised freedom to all who served
options.misconception: Congress made no such promise in 1775; it was Dunmore, the British governor, who first offered freedom for service.

rationales.B: Virginia's enslaved workers were the colony's labor force and a source of soldiers. Background: between 800 and 2,000 enslaved people reached Dunmore, and each side feared the other would gain them first.
rationales.A: Agreement is the opposite of what the passages show; the two sides fight over enslaved people, not over ending slavery.
rationales.C: No Parliamentary order lies behind either passage; Dunmore and Virginia each act for their own war aims.
rationales.D: Congress promised nothing of the kind in 1775; the freedom offer came from the British governor, not from Congress.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what enslaved people were worth in wartime. Workers for farms and soldiers for armies.
2. Ask what each side feared. Dunmore feared too few men; Virginia feared losing its labor force to him.
3. Read the offers as bids. Freedom for service against pardon for return — each side paying for loyalty.
Remember: when enemies both court the same people, those people hold power — ask what each side is buying.
